clinicalPearls: Acrocyanosis is a painless, persistent, symmetrical blue-purple discolouration of the hands and feet caused by vasospasm of small cutaneous arteries and arterioles with secondary dilatation of the subpapillary venous plexus.
It is distinguished from Raynaud phenomenon by its continuous rather than episodic nature and the absence of the sharply demarcated triphasic white-blue-red colour change.
Affected extremities are typically cold and clammy with associated hyperhidrosis, yet peripheral pulses are normal and there is no ulceration, pain or trophic change in the primary form.
Primary (idiopathic) acrocyanosis is benign, more common in young women, worsened by cold and emotional stress, and often improves in warm environments and with age.
Secondary acrocyanosis may reflect connective-tissue disease, cryoglobulinaemia, antiphospholipid syndrome, malignancy, anorexia nervosa, or drugs, and warrants a search for an underlying disorder.
Central cyanosis from hypoxaemia must be excluded, as acrocyanosis is purely peripheral and does not affect the tongue or mucous membranes; oxygen saturation is normal in the primary form.
Diascopy and warming help confirm the vasomotor nature, and the discolouration blanches with elevation of the limb, distinguishing it from fixed vascular occlusion.
Reassurance, cold avoidance and warmth are the mainstays of management for primary disease; vasodilators are rarely needed and pharmacotherapy is generally unsatisfactory.
reference.pathophysiology: Acrocyanosis results from persistent vasospasm of the small arterioles and cutaneous arteries supplying the acral skin, causing reduced arterial inflow and sluggish capillary perfusion. Compensatory dilatation of the subpapillary venous plexuses leads to pooling of slow-flowing, deoxygenated blood, which produces the sustained bluish discolouration and the associated coolness and sweating. Unlike Raynaud phenomenon, the vasoconstriction is continuous rather than paroxysmal and does not fully occlude flow, so tissue viability is preserved and ischaemic complications do not occur in the primary form. Increased vasomotor tone, heightened sensitivity to cold, and in some cases increased blood viscosity or circulating cryoproteins in secondary disease all contribute. The precise trigger of the primary form is unknown but is thought to reflect a functional abnormality of local vascular reactivity.
additionalDifferentials: Peripheral cyanosis from central hypoxaemia or cardiac disease
additionalInvestigations: Pulse oximetry and, if indicated, arterial blood gas to exclude central cyanosis
Nailfold capillaroscopy to help differentiate from connective-tissue disease
Autoimmune serology including antinuclear and antiphospholipid antibodies
Full blood count and assessment of blood viscosity/paraproteins
Doppler studies and palpation of peripheral pulses to confirm patent large vessels
Screening for occult malignancy or eating disorder where clinically suggested
redFlags: Digital ulceration, necrosis or pain suggesting a secondary occlusive or ischaemic process
Asymmetry or involvement of a single digit indicating structural arterial disease
Central cyanosis with low oxygen saturation pointing to cardiopulmonary pathology
Systemic features of connective-tissue disease or cryoglobulinaemia
Rapid onset in an older patient raising concern for underlying malignancy
reference.prognosis: Primary acrocyanosis is a benign, chronic condition that does not threaten limb viability and frequently improves with warmth and increasing age. The outlook in secondary disease depends on the underlying disorder.
pitfalls: Confusing continuous acrocyanosis with episodic Raynaud phenomenon and pursuing the wrong work-up
Overlooking central cyanosis by assuming all peripheral blueness is acrocyanosis
Missing a secondary cause such as cryoglobulinaemia, antiphospholipid syndrome or occult malignancy
Attributing unilateral or single-digit discolouration to acrocyanosis when it indicates arterial occlusion
Failing to consider anorexia nervosa in a young patient with cold, cyanotic extremities
management: Reassurance in primary disease, which is benign and does not threaten limb viability
Conservative measures — cold avoidance, keeping the extremities warm, and smoking cessation
A trial of vasodilators such as calcium-channel blockers for troublesome cases, though benefit is limited
Identify and treat any underlying cause in secondary disease, including connective-tissue disease, cryoglobulinaemia, antiphospholipid syndrome, malignancy, anorexia nervosa or drugs
Exclude central cyanosis from hypoxaemia before attributing the discolouration to peripheral vasospasm
